standard.title: Migration and Australian society
standard.description: the motivation of people migrating to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, their stories and effects on Australian society, including migrants from the Asia region
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5K03 (Individuals and groups in colonial development): Students understand the contributions and experiences of different groups in colonial Australia, including some migrant groups. Students understand historical significance and multi-perspective analysis.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the motivations of people who migrated to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, describe their stories and experiences, and assess the effects of migration on Australian society, including contributions of migrants from the Asia region.

nodes.label: Push and pull factors for migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the push and pull factors that have motivated people to migrate to Australia since Federation, including economic factors, conflict and political refuge.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two push factors and two pull factors that have driven migration to Australia and give one historical example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the push and pull factors that have driven migration to Australia since Federation: economic push factors (poverty, unemployment), conflict and political instability as push factors, and Australia's economic opportunities, political stability and immigration programs as pull factors. Apply to specific 20th century migrant groups (e.g. post-WWII Europeans, South-East Asian refugees, Assisted Passage).
wider: Compare the push and pull factors for two different migrant groups from different eras (e.g. post-WWII European migrants and South-East Asian refugees) and explain why their motivations differed
Investigate a specific immigration program (e.g. the Assisted Passage Migration scheme, Refugee and Humanitarian Program) and assess how it shaped who migrated and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish push from pull factors will describe migration as a single undifferentiated movement. The push/pull distinction is the analytical foundation for understanding why specific groups migrated when they did.

response_modes.reason: Use a push/pull T-chart with specific examples for at least two different migrant groups before moving to analysis. Visual scaffolding makes the distinction clear and avoids conflation.

success_criteria: Students identify at least two push factors and two pull factors for migration to Australia.
Students apply push/pull factors to at least one specific historical migrant group.

nodes.label: Stories and experiences of migrants
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the journeys and experiences of migrants to Australia using primary sources including letters, documents, oral histories and objects, explaining the circumstances of arrival and early settlement.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the journey and early experience of one migrant or migrant group using information from at least one primary source.
nodes.typical_width: Explore individual narratives using primary sources (letters, documents, historical objects, oral histories) to describe the journey, circumstances of arrival, and early experience of migrants to Australia from different groups and time periods.
wider: Conduct or analyse an oral history interview with a person from a migrant family (including family history connections) and present their migration story
Examine population data from different points in time to trace how the places of birth of Australia's people have changed, and connect this data to historical migration patterns

response_modes.reason: Individual migration stories are the key humanising layer for the push/pull analysis — students need to hear diverse stories across different groups and time periods rather than a single 'representative' narrative.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Oral history and family history investigation is a rich primary source skill with personal connection potential — the elaborations explicitly support this direction and it has significant motivational and cultural value.
success_criteria: Students describe the migration experience of at least one individual or group using primary source evidence.
Students identify at least two specific details from primary sources in their description.

nodes.label: Effects of migration on Australian society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of migration on Australian society, including cultural changes, economic contributions and social impacts, with specific reference to contributions from migrant groups including those from the Asia region.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two effects of migration on Australian society and give a specific example for each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how migration has changed Australian society: cultural practices related to family life, beliefs and customs; contributions to industries (e.g. cattle, Snowy Mountains Scheme, pearling); contributions from notable Australians of migrant background; and the influence of Asian migration on Australian culture and society.
wider: Investigate the role of a specific cultural group in Australia's economic or social development and assess the significance of their contribution
Evaluate how Australian multicultural identity today reflects the history of migration since Federation, using contemporary data and examples

response_modes.reason: The effects of migration are best understood across multiple domains (cultural, economic, social) and multiple migrant groups — students who focus only on one group or one domain miss the cumulative picture.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two effects of migration on Australian society.
Students give specific examples from at least one migrant group, including from the Asia region.

nodes.label: Migration as a shaping force in Australian history
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the motivations, stories and effects of migration since Federation have shaped Australian society, assessing migration's role as a significant force in Australia's social and cultural development.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how migration has shaped Australian society by drawing on examples of motivation, individual stories and societal effects.
nodes.typical_width: Assess migration as a shaping force in Australian society — connecting motivations (push/pull), individual stories, and societal effects into a coherent explanation of how migration since Federation has contributed to Australia's identity, economy and culture.
wider: Evaluate how government migration policies have shaped the composition and character of Australian society, assessing both intended and unintended social effects
Compare the experience of recent migrants to Australia with those from earlier 20th century waves of migration, identifying what has changed and what remains similar

response_modes.reason: The integration requires connecting the analytical framework (push/pull), the human scale (stories), and the social scale (effects) into a coherent historical argument. Use a structured essay or presentation framework.

success_criteria: Students explain migration motivations, describe migrant experiences, and assess effects on Australian society in an integrated account.
Students reference specific migrant groups including those from the Asia region.
Students use relevant terms (e.g. 'push factor', 'pull factor', 'refugee', 'multiculturalism') accurately.
